title: Logs and monitoring
intro: A production application can be running while users are experiencing errors, slow responses, or broken workflows. Logs and monitoring give you the evidence needed to understand what is happening, detect problems early, and decide when an incident actually needs attention.
body:
## Why logs and monitoring matter

In development, you can often reproduce a problem by opening IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition, putting a breakpoint in the code, and stepping through the application. Production is different.

A production application is running somewhere you may not be able to inspect interactively. Multiple users may be making requests at the same time, containers may restart, and a problem may disappear before you can reproduce it locally.

This is why production systems need **observability**. Observability means collecting useful information about the internal state and behaviour of a system from the outside.

Three common sources are:

- **Logs** describe individual events and provide detailed context.
- **Metrics** represent numerical measurements over time.
- **Traces** connect work across services and requests.

This lesson focuses primarily on logs and metrics, with a brief look at frontend error reporting.

A useful production flow is:

~~~text
Application
   |
   +--> structured logs
   |
   +--> metrics
   |
   +--> health checks
   |
   v
Monitoring system
   |
   v
Alerts + dashboards
~~~

The goal is not to collect everything. The goal is to collect information that helps you answer useful questions when something goes wrong.

---

## Log levels

A log level communicates the importance or severity of an event.

A common ordering is:

~~~text
debug < info < warn < error
~~~

### DEBUG

`DEBUG` is useful for detailed information during development or troubleshooting.

~~~text
DEBUG Loading product 42 from repository
~~~

Debug logging can become extremely noisy at production traffic levels, so it is often disabled or restricted in production.

### INFO

`INFO` records normal, meaningful application events.

~~~text
INFO Order created successfully
~~~

Examples include application startup, important lifecycle events, or successful operations where an audit trail is useful.

### WARN

`WARN` indicates something unexpected or potentially problematic, but the application can continue operating.

~~~text
WARN External payment provider responded slowly
~~~

A warning should usually be actionable. If something is expected and harmless, it probably does not need to be logged as a warning.

### ERROR

`ERROR` indicates a failure that requires investigation or attention.

~~~text
ERROR Failed to process payment
~~~

An error should contain enough context to understand what failed without exposing secrets or sensitive data.

The configured log level normally determines which messages are emitted. If the logger is configured at `INFO`, debug messages are skipped while info, warning, and error messages are written.

---

## Why structured logs are better

A traditional log line might look like:

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Plain text log", "lang": "text", "code": "2026-10-04 10:12:01 ERROR Order failed for user 7 after 1840ms", "note": "Readable, but you can only grep it."}, "right": {"title": "Structured JSON", "lang": "json", "code": "{\"time\":\"2026-10-04T10:12:01Z\",\"level\":\"ERROR\",\n \"message\":\"Order failed\",\"userId\":7,\n \"durationMs\":1840,\"requestId\":\"a1b2\"}", "note": "Filter, count and chart by any field."}}
~~~

~~~text
2026-10-04 12:15:20 ERROR Failed to create order for user 42
~~~

This is readable, but machines have to parse the text to understand which part represents the timestamp, level, message, or user identifier.

A structured JSON log can represent the same event as:

~~~json
{"time":"2026-10-04T12:15:20Z","level":"error","message":"Failed to create order","orderId":"42"}
~~~

Now a log aggregation system can easily search for:

~~~text
level = error
orderId = 42
~~~

Structured logs are especially useful once you have multiple containers or services.

In Spring Boot, Logback is commonly used as the logging implementation. A JSON encoder such as the Logstash Logback Encoder can format log events as JSON.

The exact configuration depends on your project, but the architecture is straightforward:

~~~text
Spring Boot
    |
    v
SLF4J logging API
    |
    v
Logback
    |
    v
JSON encoder
    |
    v
stdout / log collector
~~~

For containerized applications, writing logs to standard output is often preferable to maintaining application-specific log files inside the container. Docker and the hosting platform can then collect those logs.

---

## Logging to standard output in containers

A Docker container should generally treat its standard output and error streams as the application's log destination.

For example, your Spring Boot application can write structured logs to stdout. Docker can then expose those logs through:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f api
~~~

You do not need to SSH into the container and search through a log file just to understand what the application is doing.

This also makes logs easier to collect in cloud environments, where the platform can forward container output to a centralized logging system.

In IntelliJ IDEA, you can inspect application output directly while developing locally. When the application is running through Docker integration, the Services tool window can also help you inspect container logs.

The principle is the same in both cases: logs should be accessible without modifying the application or attaching a debugger to production.

---

## Correlation and request IDs

Imagine a user reports that checkout failed. The request passes through a frontend, API, database, and possibly an external payment provider.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "One request id across the stack", "nodes": [{"id": "fe", "label": "React", "sub": "X-Request-Id: a1b2", "kind": "client"}, {"id": "api", "label": "API filter", "sub": "MDC.put(requestId)", "kind": "server", "highlight": true}, {"id": "svc", "label": "Service logs", "sub": "requestId=a1b2"}, {"id": "db", "label": "Slow query log", "sub": "requestId=a1b2", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "q", "label": "Search requestId=a1b2", "sub": "the whole story", "kind": "queue", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "fe", "to": "api"}, {"from": "api", "to": "svc"}, {"from": "svc", "to": "db"}, {"from": "svc", "to": "q", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

If every log line is unrelated, finding the relevant events can be difficult.

A **correlation ID**, often called a request ID, gives a request a unique identifier that can be included in related log entries.

For example:

~~~json
{"level":"info","message":"Request started","requestId":"abc-123","path":"/api/orders"}
{"level":"info","message":"Creating order","requestId":"abc-123","orderId":"42"}
{"level":"error","message":"Payment failed","requestId":"abc-123","orderId":"42"}
~~~

You can now search for `requestId = abc-123` and see the complete story.

In Java applications, **MDC**, or Mapped Diagnostic Context, is commonly used to attach contextual values to logging events.

Conceptually:

~~~java
MDC.put("requestId", requestId);
try {
    // Handle request
} finally {
    MDC.remove("requestId");
}
~~~

The cleanup is important because application servers reuse threads. Context from one request must not accidentally appear in another request's logs.

In a Spring Boot application, a servlet filter or interceptor is a natural place to create or propagate a request ID.

---

## What you should never log

Logs are operational data, but that does not make them a safe place for everything.

Never casually log:

- Passwords.
- JWTs or access tokens.
- Authorization headers.
- Database passwords.
- API keys.
- Encryption keys.
- Payment credentials.
- Sensitive personal information that is not needed for troubleshooting.

For example, this is dangerous:

~~~text
ERROR Login failed password=MyRealPassword
~~~

Even if application access is restricted, logs are often copied to other systems, retained for longer periods, and accessible to more people than the production database.

A better approach is to log safe metadata:

~~~json
{"level":"warn","message":"Login failed","emailDomain":"example.com","requestId":"abc-123"}
~~~

Even apparently harmless identifiers should be considered carefully. Logging an internal database ID may be useful; logging a complete customer record usually is not.

A good rule is:

**If the application does not need the value to diagnose the problem, do not put it in the log.**

Sensitive fields should also be redacted automatically when possible. For example, a logging utility can replace values associated with keys such as `password`, `token`, `authorization`, and `secret` with `[REDACTED]`.

---

## Spring Boot Actuator

Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational endpoints that help you understand the state of the application.

One of the most useful endpoints is:

~~~text
/actuator/health
~~~

A healthy application can return information indicating that it is ready to serve requests.

Actuator can also expose metrics and other operational information depending on the configured endpoints.

The important security principle is that operational endpoints should not automatically be exposed publicly. Some endpoints can reveal information that should only be available to administrators or monitoring infrastructure.

A production architecture might look like:

~~~text
Public internet
      |
      v
Application API
      |
      +--> /actuator/health
      |
      +--> metrics endpoint
               |
               v
        monitoring system
~~~

The health endpoint can be used for readiness and liveness checks, while metrics provide longer-term numerical information about the application.

---

## Metrics with Micrometer

A log tells you that one event happened. A metric lets you understand patterns across many events.

For example, instead of logging every request and manually counting them, you can expose a request counter and latency measurements.

Spring Boot commonly integrates with **Micrometer**, an application metrics facade that supports multiple monitoring systems.

A simplified architecture is:

~~~text
Spring Boot
    |
    v
Micrometer
    |
    v
Prometheus
    |
    v
Grafana
~~~

**Prometheus** collects and stores metrics in a time-series format. **Grafana** can visualize those metrics in dashboards and can also participate in alerting workflows.

You do not need to understand every Prometheus query before using this stack. Start by understanding what you are measuring and why.

Useful metrics might include:

- Request count.
- Request duration.
- Error count.
- JVM memory usage.
- CPU usage.
- Database connection pool usage.
- Active HTTP requests.

Metrics should describe behaviour that helps you make operational decisions.

---

## The four golden signals

A widely used monitoring model is the **four golden signals**:

~~~terms
[{"term": "Latency", "def": "How long requests take — watch p95, not the average."}, {"term": "Traffic", "def": "How many requests per second."}, {"term": "Errors", "def": "Share of failed requests (5xx)."}, {"term": "Saturation", "def": "How full the system is: CPU, memory, DB connections."}]
~~~

1. Latency.
2. Traffic.
3. Errors.
4. Saturation.

### Latency

Latency measures how long requests take.

Average latency can hide serious problems. Suppose most requests take 100 ms but a small percentage take 10 seconds. The average might still look acceptable.

That is why percentiles are useful.

**p95 latency** means that approximately 95% of observed requests are at or below that latency, while the slowest 5% are above it.

For example:

~~~text
p95 = 420 ms
~~~

means the 95th percentile of measured requests is around 420 milliseconds.

### Traffic

Traffic measures how much demand the system receives.

For an HTTP API, this might be requests per second.

A sudden traffic increase can explain increased CPU usage or latency even when no deployment occurred.

### Errors

Errors measure failed operations. Depending on the system, this might include HTTP 5xx responses, failed background jobs, or other application-specific failures.

Error rate is often more useful than raw error count because it accounts for traffic volume.

For example:

~~~text
errors = 50
requests = 1000
error rate = 5%
~~~

### Saturation

Saturation measures how close a resource is to its capacity.

Examples include:

- CPU utilization.
- Memory pressure.
- Database connection pool usage.
- Disk capacity.
- Queue depth.

A system with increasing saturation may be approaching a failure point even if users have not noticed a problem yet.

---

## Error rate and p95 latency

Two particularly useful application indicators are error rate and p95 latency.

Suppose your API receives 10,000 requests:

~~~text
10,000 total requests
   250 failed requests

error rate = 250 / 10,000 = 2.5%
~~~

Now suppose p95 latency is 850 ms. That tells you a significant portion of users are experiencing slower responses than you might expect.

These values can be displayed in a dashboard:

~~~text
Requests:       10,000
Error rate:       2.5%
p95 latency:      850 ms
CPU:               72%
DB pool:            65%
~~~

The dashboard is useful because it gives you a quick overview. Logs can then provide the detailed evidence needed to investigate an anomaly.

This illustrates an important relationship:

~~~text
Metrics tell you that something is wrong.
Logs help explain why.
~~~

---

## Alerts should be actionable

An alert should cause someone to do something.

A bad alert might say:

~~~text
CPU is 70%
~~~

If 70% CPU is normal for your application, this alert creates noise.

A more useful alert might be:

~~~text
API error rate has exceeded 5% for 10 minutes
~~~

Now someone can investigate an actual service-quality problem.

Good alerts should have:

- A clear condition.
- A meaningful threshold.
- A suitable time window.
- A responsible team or person.
- Enough context to start investigating.

Avoid creating alerts for every unusual event. If operators receive hundreds of low-value notifications, they eventually stop trusting alerts.

An alert should answer the question: **What action should someone take because this condition is true?**

---

## Frontend error reporting

Backend logs cannot tell you everything about a user's browser.

A frontend can fail because of:

- JavaScript runtime errors.
- Browser-specific behaviour.
- Network failures.
- Failed API requests.
- Unexpected application state.
- Asset loading problems.

A frontend error-reporting service can capture browser errors, stack traces, release versions, and useful context.

The same security rules apply here. Do not send passwords, access tokens, payment information, or unnecessary personal data to the error-reporting platform.

A useful frontend error event might contain:

~~~json
{
  "message":"Failed to load products",
  "release":"2026.10.04",
  "path":"/products",
  "requestId":"abc-123"
}
~~~

The request ID is especially useful because it can connect a frontend failure to the corresponding backend logs.

---

## Reading logs with Docker Compose

When the application runs through Docker Compose, the first place to look is often:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f api
~~~

You can also inspect all services:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f
~~~

Suppose the API fails during startup. Look for:

~~~text
ERROR
Caused by:
Exception
Failed
Connection refused
~~~

Do not stop at the last line automatically. Java stack traces often contain the root cause earlier or deeper in the exception chain.

For example, an application might report that Spring failed to create a bean, while the underlying cause is actually a database connection failure.

The useful debugging sequence is:

~~~text
Which service failed?
       |
       v
Which operation failed?
       |
       v
What is the first meaningful exception?
       |
       v
What configuration or dependency caused it?
~~~

---

## Reading logs in IntelliJ IDEA

During development, IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition gives you immediate access to application output when you run the Spring Boot application.

If you run the Docker Compose environment through Docker integration, the Services tool window can also help you inspect container state and logs.

Use this feedback loop:

~~~text
change code
   -> run application
   -> inspect logs
   -> reproduce behaviour
   -> fix code
~~~

A developer should become comfortable reading logs rather than treating them as an intimidating wall of text.

Look first for the timestamp, severity, request or correlation ID, operation name, and exception cause. Structured JSON makes these fields much easier to search and filter once logs are centralized.

---

## Common mistakes

### Logging everything

More logs do not automatically mean better observability. Excessive logging increases storage costs, makes important events harder to find, and can expose sensitive information.

### Logging secrets

Passwords, tokens, authorization headers, and secrets should never appear in ordinary application logs. Redaction should be a defence in depth, not an excuse to log sensitive data unnecessarily.

### Using only average latency

Average latency can hide slow requests. Percentiles such as p95 provide a better view of the user experience for the slower portion of traffic.

### Creating noisy alerts

An alert that fires constantly is not useful. Tune thresholds and time windows around actual service-level expectations.

### Exposing Actuator endpoints publicly

Operational endpoints can contain sensitive information. Expose only what is required and protect management endpoints appropriately.

### Forgetting request context

Without a request or correlation ID, following one request through several services can be unnecessarily difficult. Add contextual identifiers consistently.

### Treating logs as a database

Logs are for operational events and diagnostics. If information must be reliably queried as business data, store it in the appropriate application database instead.

---

## A practical monitoring strategy

You do not need a massive observability platform on the first day.

For the course project, start with a small set of reliable capabilities:

~~~text
1. Structured application logs
2. Request/correlation IDs
3. Secret redaction
4. /actuator/health
5. Basic HTTP and JVM metrics
6. Error rate dashboard
7. p95 latency dashboard
8. One or two actionable alerts
9. Frontend error reporting
~~~

Once those pieces work, you can add distributed tracing, more detailed dashboards, log retention policies, synthetic monitoring, and more sophisticated alerting when the application actually needs them.

The professional goal is not to collect the maximum amount of telemetry. It is to make failures understandable.

When a user reports that checkout failed, you should be able to move from the frontend error to a request ID, from the request ID to backend logs, from the logs to metrics, and from the metrics to the operational impact.

That is what useful observability looks like.
takeaways: Use log levels deliberately and prefer structured JSON logs so machines can search and aggregate events reliably.
Correlation IDs and MDC make it possible to follow a request across application components.
Never log passwords, tokens, authorization headers, secrets, or unnecessary sensitive personal data.
Actuator health endpoints and Micrometer metrics provide operational signals that complement detailed logs.
The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation; p95 latency and error rate are especially useful application indicators.
Alerts should be actionable, and frontend errors should be connected to backend diagnostics whenever possible.

quiz.question: Why are structured JSON logs useful in production?
options: They make application code execute faster
They automatically encrypt all log data
They make fields such as level, request ID, and status easier for machines to search and aggregate
They eliminate the need for metrics
quiz.explanation: Structured logs represent important information as fields, allowing log collection systems to filter, search, aggregate, and analyze events reliably.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a correlation or request ID?
options: To connect related log events belonging to the same request or operation
quiz.explanation: A correlation ID can be attached to related log entries so that operators can follow a request across filters, services, and operations.

quiz.question: Which of the following should normally never be written to application logs?
quiz.explanation: Passwords, tokens, authorization headers, and similar secrets should not be logged because logs can be retained, copied, and accessed by systems or people who should not see the secret.

quiz.question: Which set contains the four golden signals?
quiz.explanation: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Together they provide a useful high-level view of service health.

quiz.question: Why can p95 latency be more useful than average latency?
options: p95 shows the latency experienced around the slower end of the request distribution
p95 is always lower than the average
quiz.explanation: Average latency can hide a smaller group of very slow requests. p95 highlights the latency at the 95th percentile and therefore gives useful information about slower user experiences.

exercise.title: Build a structured logger and log summary
exercise.task:
Define exactly these two functions:

1. `function createLogger(opts: { level: "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"; now: () => string; write: (line: string) => void })` — return an object containing exactly the logging methods `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, and `child`. Each logging method takes `(message: string, fields?: Record<string, unknown>)`. When the method's level is at or above the configured logger level, call `write` exactly once with `JSON.stringify(...)` of an object containing `{ time: now(), level, message, ...fields, ...context }`. The level order is `debug < info < warn < error`. The context comes from `child(fields)`, which returns a new logger with those child fields merged into the parent context; child fields override parent fields with the same key. Any key named `password`, `token`, `authorization`, or `secret`, case-insensitively, must have its value written as `"[REDACTED]"`.

2. `function summarize(lines: string[])` — parse JSON log lines and skip invalid JSON. Parsed lines that contain a numeric `status` count toward `total`. A status of at least 500 counts toward `errors`. Return `{ total, errors, errorRate, p95 }`, where `errorRate` is `errors / total` rounded to 3 decimal places and is `0` when `total` is zero. Collect numeric `durationMs` values independently of whether the line has a status. Sort durations ascending and calculate p95 using nearest rank: `Math.ceil(0.95 * n) - 1`. Return `null` for `p95` when there are no durations.

Do not mutate the input options, context objects, or arrays.
exercise.hint: For `createLogger`, keep a numeric level map so lower-severity messages can be skipped. Build a new context for every child instead of modifying the parent. The output order should follow `time`, `level`, `message`, fields, then context, so context overrides fields. Redact sensitive keys before serializing, including nested objects if necessary. For `summarize`, count only numeric statuses toward `total`, collect numeric durations independently, sort them numerically, and use the nearest-rank index exactly as specified.

tests.name: It writes only messages at or above the configured level
It includes timestamp, level, message, and fields
It calls write exactly once for an emitted log
It creates child context without mutating the parent
It lets child fields override parent context
It redacts sensitive keys case-insensitively
It redacts sensitive keys inside child context
It summarizes status counts and error rate
It skips invalid JSON lines
It calculates nearest-rank p95 from sorted durations
It handles missing durations and an empty input
